entries.question: Does Abandoned Hall's ability trigger if the spell is countered?
entries.text:
No.
Abandoned Hall's ability triggers "when a player plays a spell," and a countered spell is not considered played.

A card is only played once the entire play process has finished in its entirety. [CR 350.1]
Abilities that trigger on playing a card fire when that act has been completed by the card's resolution; [CR 419.4.a] if a game effect prevents resolution — for example because the spell was countered — the card is not considered to have been played and no abilities that trigger on playing cards fire. [CR 419.4.b]
This follows directly from what countering does: a countered card is cleared from the chain and is not considered to have been played. [CR 425.1.b]

entries.question: Can a unit replayed here by a spell be chosen by Abandoned Hall's triggered ability?
entries.text:
Yes.
Spells like Arcane Shift and Thrill of the Hunt add the unit to the chain as a pending item during their own resolution, pausing its play process while the spell continues. [CR 354.2] [CR 354.3]
Abandoned Hall's triggered ability does not fire until the spell has been fully played, [CR 350.1] so it is appended to the chain after the unit. [CR 383.2.c]
Because pending items are finalized in the order they were appended, [CR 337.1.b] the unit is finalized and placed on the board first — resolving immediately on finalization [CR 337.1.c] — before the triggered ability's target is chosen.
By that point the unit is already present at Abandoned Hall and is a valid choice for the buff.

### Resolution Sequence

Taking Arcane Shift as an example:

1. "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board
2. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [CR 354.2] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving [CR 354.3]
3. Arcane Shift finishes resolving and is banished; the spell is now fully played [CR 350.1]
4. HOT — cleanups run; Abandoned Hall's trigger condition is evaluated after the spell was processed [CR 383.2.c] and the triggered ability is appended to the chain as a pending item, after the unit
5. FEPR — pending items are finalized in the order they were appended; [CR 337.1.b] the unit comes first, resolves immediately upon finalization, [CR 337.1.c] and is placed at Abandoned Hall
6. Abandoned Hall's triggered ability is finalized next; you choose a target — the replayed unit is now present here and is a valid choice

Abandoned Hall's triggered ability therefore fires after the spell resolves, not when it is placed on the chain. [CR 383.2.c]
By the time the trigger condition is met, the unit is already present at Abandoned Hall and is a valid choice for the buff.

entries.question: Does the enemy Dazzling Aurora I take control of with Akshan also trigger at the end of this turn?
entries.text:
No — you gain control of it too late in the turn for its trigger to fire.

Dazzling Aurora's trigger condition is "At the end of your turn."
"At" identifies a triggered ability keyed to a specific point in time during the turn sequence [CR 383.1] — here, the Ending Step, when end-of-turn game effects take place. [CR 317.1] [CR 317.1.a]
A trigger's condition is evaluated once, immediately after that point in time is reached [CR 383.2.c] — it is not re-checked continuously for as long as the game remains in the Ending Phase.

Akshan's own play effect only triggers once he is finalized on the board — a separate, later event [CR 383.4.a] [CR 383.4.a.2] — and that is when you gain control of the enemy's Dazzling Aurora.

By the time that happens, your Ending Step's "at the end of your turn" condition has already been evaluated — once, for whatever you controlled at that instant.
The enemy Dazzling Aurora wasn't yours yet then, so it never gets checked this turn; there's no second check waiting for it later in the phase.
It will trigger normally at the end of your future turns, for as long as you continue to control it.

entries.question: Your opponent plays their own Akshan and takes control of the gear your Akshan already controls. What happens when one or both Akshans die?
entries.text:
Whichever Akshan was played most recently determines control of the gear for as long as it remains on the board.

Both Akshans generate a continuous effect that changes the gear's controller — an inherent trait of every game object. [CR 472.1] [CR 472.1.a]
Since both effects operate in the same layer and neither depends on the other, [CR 473] they are ordered by timestamp: the earliest-established effect applies first, and the most recently established effect applies last, winning out. [CR 475] [CR 475.3]
Your opponent's Akshan was played after yours, so it carries the later timestamp — its control effect is the final one applied, and your opponent controls the gear.

When an Akshan leaves the board, its "until I leave the board" duration ends and its control effect ceases immediately.
The remaining effects are then re-evaluated in timestamp order:

- Your opponent's Akshan dies: their effect ceases.
Only your Akshan's effect remains, giving you control of the gear.
- Your Akshan dies: your effect ceases.
Your opponent's Akshan's effect was already the deciding one — they continue to control the gear unchanged.
- Both Akshans die: both effects cease.
Control reverts to your opponent, since it was their gear to begin with.
If the gear is unattached and now finds itself in a base it doesn't belong to, it will be recalled to your opponent's base during the next cleanup.

entries.question: What if my unit's might is reduced before Alpha Strike resolves?
entries.text:
If the friendly unit's might is reduced between finalization and resolution, the total damage pool shrinks accordingly.
If the reduced might is now less than the number of chosen enemy unit targets, there is no longer enough damage to assign at least 1 to every target.
In that case, you must drop the minimum number of targets such that the number of remaining targets equals the friendly unit's current might — you cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage on fewer units. [CR 355.14.h]

Any effects that triggered as a result of those units being chosen as targets have already happened and are unaffected by the removal. [CR 355.14.i]

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
You chose 5 enemy units, targeting your friendly unit with 5 might.
 Before Alpha Strike resolves, your opponent plays a Reaction spell that reduces your unit's might by 2, leaving it at 3 might.
 You now have only 3 damage to distribute but 5 targets.
 You must drop 2 targets of your choice.
 The remaining 3 targets each receive at least 1 of the 3 available damage.

callouts.title: You cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage
callouts.text:
You chose 3 enemy 1 might Recruits at finalization with a friendly 3 might unit.
 Before resolution, your opponent reduces your unit's might by 1 with Stupefy (leaving it at 2 might) and buffs one of their Recruits to 2 might with En Garde.
 You now have 2 damage to distribute but 3 targets.
 You must drop exactly 1 target — leaving 2 remaining targets that each receive at least 1 damage.
 You cannot drop 2 targets to leave only the 2 might Recruit and assign both damage to it.

entries.question: When is the damage distribution decided?
entries.text:
The distribution of damage across the chosen enemy units is decided at resolution, not at finalization. [CR 355.14.e]

The total damage available equals the friendly unit's effective might when Alpha Strike resolves — meaning any Reaction speed buffs or debuffs applied by either player between finalization and resolution will affect the damage pool.

Each chosen target must receive at least 1 damage. [CR 355.14.f] [CR 355.14.g]
Beyond that minimum, you are free to assign as much damage as you like to any target, as long as the total does not exceed the friendly unit's might and every target receives at least 1.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
You chose 3 enemy units at finalization.
 When Alpha Strike resolves, your friendly unit has 6 might.
 You must assign at least 1 damage to each of the 3 targets.
 The remaining 3 damage can go wherever you choose — 4/1/1, 2/2/2, 1/1/4, and so on.

entries.question: How are targets chosen when playing Alpha Strike?
entries.text:
When finalising Alpha Strike on the chain, you declare two groups of targets:

1. The friendly unit — chosen explicitly as a standard target.
2. Up to N enemy units at battlefields, where N equals the chosen friendly unit's current might at the moment of finalization. [CR 355.14.a] [CR 355.14.b] [CR 355.14.c]
Each chosen enemy unit is a target. You may choose fewer than N, including zero. [CR 355.13]

Since each chosen enemy unit is a target of Alpha Strike, Deflect is added as a mandatory additional cost for any of those units that have it during finalization. [CR 356.2.a.2] [CR 809.1.d]

All choices are locked in at finalization and cannot be changed after this step. [CR 355.15]

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
You play Alpha Strike and choose a friendly unit with 4 might.
 You may then choose up to 4 enemy units at battlefields as the split targets.
 You choose 3.
 Those 3 units — and the friendly unit — are all locked in as targets.

entries.question: Can I use Arcane Shift to banish my only unit at a battlefield and replay it there?
entries.text:
Yes, as long as you control the battlefield.

When Arcane Shift resolves, the replayed unit sits on the chain as a pending item throughout the cleanup that follows.
Because a chain exists, the turn is in a closed state, and cleanup step 4 — which would make the battlefield uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [CR 323.6]
The battlefield stays controlled, and when the pending unit is finalized you can choose to replay it there.
Attackers cannot replay their unit to the attacking battlefield because they never control it in the first place.

### How Arcane Shift Resolves

When Arcane Shift resolves, the following happens:

1. "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board
2. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [CR 354.2] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving [CR 354.3]
3. "Deal 3 to an enemy unit" and "Banish this" both resolve
4. Arcane Shift finishes resolving, queuing one or more cleanups as Outstanding Tasks
5. HOT — the cleanups run; the pending unit keeps the chain alive, so the turn remains in a closed state [CR 309.1] and cleanup step 4 [CR 323.6] does not fire
6. FEPR — once all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized; [CR 335.2] you choose where to play it, and the battlefield is still under your control

entries.question: If the spell that receives Astral Heron's discount is later countered, is the discount granted to a different card instead?
entries.text:
No — the discount is spent the moment it reduces that spell's cost.

Astral Heron's triggered ability resolves into a delayed passive ability, active only for "your next card" — a single specified window, not a standing effect. [CR 391]
That window belongs to finalizing the next card, not to that card resolving successfully — it doesn't linger to see whether the spell goes on to succeed.
Discounts are applied while determining a card's total cost, in step 3 of the play process, and the reduced cost is paid in step 4 — both steps happen well before the card is even finalized, let alone placed on the chain where it could be countered. [CR 356.4] [CR 356.4.a] [CR 357]
Whichever card is played next consumes that window the moment its cost is reduced; nothing that happens to that card afterward can reopen it.

A countered card does nothing and is not considered to have been played, [CR 425.1.a] [CR 425.1.b] and countering does not refund any costs paid to play it, additional costs included. [CR 425.1.c] [CR 425.1.c.1]
That confirms the reduced cost itself stays spent — but Astral Heron's discount was already used up before the spell was even vulnerable to being countered, so there was never anything left to give to a different card.

entries.question: If Astral Heron is killed or moved away in response to its own trigger, does the cost reduction still apply?
entries.text:
Yes — the discount still applies to your next card.

Once Astral Heron's triggered ability is already a chain item, waiting to resolve, killing or moving Astral Heron in response to it changes nothing about how it resolves.

"If I'm at a battlefield" is an intervening if, so it's only checked once, at the moment the triggering event occurs, to decide whether the ability is placed on the chain at all — it is not re-checked when the ability later resolves. [CR 383.3.e]
Once triggered, the ability is an independent item on the chain, and nothing in its effect references Astral Heron's location or continued presence, so there's no referent left for a later removal to invalidate.

So an opponent reacting to the trigger by killing, bouncing, or moving Astral Heron before it resolves doesn't stop the reduction: the trigger condition and intervening if were already satisfied the moment the ability went on the chain, and it resolves exactly as if nothing had happened.

entries.question: Does Astral Heron's ability trigger if it's your first card played to a battlefield this turn?
entries.text:
Yes — assuming it's played to a battlefield.

Play, in a trigger condition, refers to a card resolving, not merely being placed on the chain. [CR 350.1] [CR 359] [CR 359.2]
Units resolve the moment they finalize: becoming a game object, gaining their active abilities, and entering the board at the chosen location, all in that same moment. [CR 359.2.a] [CR 359.2.c]

A trigger's condition is evaluated after a potentially inciting event has been processed, and nothing requires that event to have been caused by a different card. [CR 383.2.c] [CR 383.2.c.1]
The ability's text splits into two parts: "When you play your first card each turn" is the trigger condition, running up to the first comma, [CR 383.2.a] and "if I'm at a battlefield" is the first thing after that comma, making it an intervening if — checked at trigger time, not on resolution. [CR 383.3.e]
Astral Heron's own resolution satisfies both parts at once: it's simultaneously an instance of "you play a card" and the moment it arrives at a battlefield.
If it's the first card played this turn and it's played to a battlefield, both are satisfied at that same moment and the ability is placed on the chain.

entries.question: If Azir is killed or returned to his base before his attack trigger resolves, do token units still move?
entries.text:
No.
"This battlefield" refers to the battlefield Azir currently occupies — that information is checked when the instruction executes.
If Azir is no longer at a battlefield at that point, the instruction is impossible and is ignored.

"This battlefield" in Azir's ability is not a target.
It is programmatically determined from Azir's current location, since he can only ever be at one battlefield at a time — no choice is ever made. [CR 355.10.d] [CR 355.10.d.1]
It is instead a referent: information drawn from the source of the ability itself. [CR 359.3.f.1]
Referents are checked at the moment the instruction executes, not when the trigger was placed on the chain. [CR 359.3.f.2]

If Azir has been moved to his base or killed before the trigger resolves, there is no "this battlefield" to move token units to.
The instruction cannot be followed and is ignored. [CR 359.3.e.6]

callouts.text:
Two common plays that produce this outcome:

- Hidden Blade, when played from Hidden, can be used in response to Azir's attack trigger to kill him at Reaction speed.
- Overzealous Fan's defend trigger fires simultaneously with Azir's attack trigger when combat designations are assigned.
 Because Azir's controller places their trigger first, Overzealous Fan's trigger sits above it on the chain and resolves first, potentially moving Azir to his base before his own trigger resolves.

In either case, "this battlefield" has no valid referent when Azir's trigger resolves and nothing happens.

entries.question: If the killed unit has Deathknell, does it resolve before or after the banished unit and its triggers?
entries.text:
After, even though it's finalized first — finalization proceeds in the order items were appended to the chain, but resolution proceeds in the opposite order, newest item first.

Baited Hook's ability resolves in its entirety without interruption, [CR 354.3] so both the killed unit's Deathknell trigger and the unit it later banishes and plays get appended to the chain as pending items during that same resolution, with the Deathknell appended first.
Once Baited Hook's ability finishes, those pending items are finalized in that same order — Deathknell first — but the chain then resolves newest-first, so anything appended after the Deathknell, including the banished unit's own triggers, resolves before it does.
The step-by-step below spells this out.

### Resolution Sequence

Killing Ruined Rex — whose Deathknell reads "Deal 4 to an enemy unit" — as an example:

1. Baited Hook's ability resolves. "Kill a friendly unit" kills Ruined Rex.
2. Ruined Rex's Deathknell trigger is added to the chain as a pending item, on top of Baited Hook's still-resolving ability. [CR 428.1.a.1.b] [CR 808.1.d.2]
3. Baited Hook's ability continues resolving: you look at the top 5 cards of your main deck and banish a unit with might up to 1 more than Ruined Rex's, then play it ignoring its cost. That unit is added to the chain as a second pending item, above the Deathknell. [CR 354.2]
4. "Then recycle the rest" executes, and Baited Hook's ability finishes resolving.
5. Two pending items remain: the Deathknell and the banished unit. They must be finalized before anything can resolve, in the order they were appended — the Deathknell first. [CR 337.1] [CR 337.1.b] Its target — the enemy unit to deal 4 to — is chosen now. [CR 355.5]
6. The banished unit finalizes next, choosing its location, then resolves immediately by entering the board. [CR 337.1.c]
7. If the banished unit has a triggered ability that fires when it's played, that ability is added to the chain now, above the Deathknell, since it was appended later. [CR 337.1.c.2]
8. Once no pending items remain, the chain resolves top-down: [CR 337.1.c.3] the banished unit's own trigger resolves first, and Ruined Rex's Deathknell — appended before any of this — resolves last, dealing its 4 damage. [CR 340.1]

entries.question: What happens if the targeted unit is removed before Baited Hook's ability resolves?
entries.text:
The unit can't be killed, and no unit can be banished from the top 5, since nothing can satisfy a might comparison against a null value.

If the friendly unit is no longer a legal target when the ability resolves — for example, if it was returned to its owner's hand in response — it is unaffected by the ability's "kill" instruction. [CR 359.3.e.2] [CR 359.3.e.5]
Because the unit was never killed, any information the ability checks about it, including its might, returns null. [CR 359.3.e.12]
"Banish a unit with might up to 1 more than the killed unit" can never be satisfied against a null might, so no unit can be chosen from among the top 5 cards, even though you still look at them.
"Then recycle the rest" is unaffected by this, since it isn't tied to the killed unit's might — you still recycle every card you looked at that wasn't banished.

entries.question: Can my opponent interact before the friendly unit is killed?
entries.text:
Yes, as killing the unit is part of the effect, not a cost, so it's a target declared when the ability is put on the chain.

"Kill a friendly unit" comes after the ":" in Baited Hook's activated ability, so it's the first instruction of the effect rather than part of the cost — an activated ability's cost is everything before the ":", and its effect is everything after. [CR 377.1]
Because it isn't a cost, the friendly unit is a normal target, chosen and declared as the ability is put on the chain. [CR 355.7] [CR 355.8]
This is the opposite of cards like Sacrifice, where "kill a friendly unit" is stated as an additional cost and is therefore excluded from targeting entirely. [CR 355.10.c] [CR 355.10.c.1]

Since the unit is targeted rather than paid as a cost, opponents get a normal opportunity to react before Baited Hook's ability resolves, just like with any other targeted ability. [CR 359.3.c]
Later in the same ability, "up to 1 more than the killed unit" references the unit affected by the earlier "kill" instruction, making the two linked instructions. [CR 359.3.e.14]
Because the unit has already moved to the trash by the time this later instruction checks it, the ability looks back at the unit's characteristics as they were immediately before it changed zones. [CR 359.3.e.13]

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
You activate Baited Hook, targeting a friendly unit with 4 might.
 In response, your opponent plays Stupefy, reducing that unit's might by 1 down to 3.
 Stupefy fully resolves before Baited Hook's ability does, so the unit already has 3 might at the moment it's killed.
 When the ability checks the killed unit's might immediately after, it looks back at that same reduced value — so you may only banish a unit with might up to 4 from among the top 5 cards of your main deck, one lower than if Stupefy hadn't been played.

Baron Nashor is entering the board for the first time (a zone change), which is not a move. [CR 441.2]

entries.question: What happens after Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit?
entries.text:
A non-combat showdown begins.
The Baron Pit is newly created and has no controller when Baron Nashor enters it.
Being played to a battlefield applies contested status to it, provided the entering unit's controller does not already control that battlefield. [CR 187.3.a.1]
Because the Baron Pit is uncontrolled at that moment, a non-combat showdown is staged during the resulting cleanup — the same mechanism that triggers when Sneaky Deckhand is played to an open battlefield. [CR 316.5.b] [CR 323.8] [CR 344.2]

If an opposing unit arrives at the Baron Pit during the showdown the non-combat showdown becomes a combat showdown. [CR 316.5.b.1.a]

If the showdown closes with only Baron Nashor's controller's units present at the Baron Pit, and they have not yet scored it this turn, they conquer it and score. [CR 348.2.a] [CR 348.2.a.1]

entries.question: Does the Baron Pit need to be scored to win by conquering?
entries.text:
Yes.
Winning by conquering at match point requires having scored every battlefield on the board that turn — including the Baron Pit. [CR 466.1.b.2]
If it hasn't been scored, the winning conquer draws a card instead.

Winning by hold is unaffected, as it has no such requirement. [CR 466.1.b.1]

entries.question: Can I play Baron Nashor while an opponent's Mageseeker Warden is at a battlefield?
entries.text:
It depends on whether the Baron Pit is already on the board.

If the Baron Pit is not yet on the board, Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit, not your base.
As Baron Nashor is played, his "as you play me" instruction fires during the playing process — the Baron Pit battlefield token is added to the board. [CR 135.2.b.3] [CR 184.9]
Under Mageseeker Warden's restriction, your base is the only valid playing location — where Baron Nashor is nominally played to — but his replacement effect overrides where he actually enters. [CR 355.2.a]
His "If you do, I enter there" then functions as a replacement effect (per Riot ruling) that intercedes when he would enter the board, replacing his entry to his base with entry to the Baron Pit. [CR 369] [CR 370.1.a]

If the Baron Pit is already on the board, the "as you play me" instruction does nothing — the Baron Pit token is only added if it's not there already — so the "If you do" condition is not met.
Baron Nashor simply enters his base, the only valid playing location under Mageseeker Warden's restriction. [CR 355.2.a]

Baron Nashor's "If you do, I enter there" lacks the "would" or "instead" language the rules use to identify replacement effects, [CR 369.1] and entry-location-modifying instructions of this form are not explicitly addressed. [CR 369.2]

entries.question: Can the opponent trigger an optional additional cost effect when playing a unit via Bone Skewer, even though its costs are ignored?
entries.text:
Yes, as declaring the intent to pay is what satisfies the condition, not the amount actually spent.

The phrase "any and all costs" in Bone Skewer's text is intentionally broader than the standard "ignoring its cost" wording.
Standard cost-ignoring only zeroes out a card's base Energy and Power costs, [CR 356.1.b.1] but "any and all" extends that to additional costs as well.
Despite this, the opponent may still declare their intention to pay an optional additional cost during step 2 of playing the card — the decision to pay is made before costs are determined.
Once declared, that additional cost is itself subject to "any and all costs" and is therefore already 0 when it comes time to pay. [CR 356.4.f]
An optional additional cost is considered paid based on the decision to pay, not the amount actually spent, [CR 356.4.f.1] so the condition is fully satisfied.
Any conditional effect tied to "if you paid the additional cost" therefore triggers normally.

 Your opponent is instructed to play Nami to the chosen battlefield, ignoring any and all costs.
 As part of that process, they declare their intention to pay the optional additional cost of Calm.
 That cost is already 0, so nothing is actually paid — but because they chose to pay it, the condition is met.
 Nami's triggered ability fires, stunning an enemy unit.

entries.question: Can targeting protection prevent the stun from Bone Skewer?
entries.text:
No, as the unit to be stunned is determined automatically, not chosen, so no targeting occurs.

When Bone Skewer's triggered ability fires — "When they do, Stun it" — the "it" refers unambiguously to the unit the opponent just played as a result of Bone Skewer's effect.
No choice is ever made about which unit is stunned; it is always and only that unit.
Because the unit is programmatically determined rather than chosen, it is not a target. [CR 355.10.d]

This means targeting protection — such as "I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities," as seen on Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor — does not prevent the stun.
Deflect is similarly irrelevant, since Deflect is only added as a cost when a spell or ability chooses an opponent's permanent, [CR 809.1.d] which is not the case here.

Passive abilities of permanents are only active while on the board, [CR 365.1] so that protection — as seen on units like Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor — has no effect while the unit is in the opponent's hand.

entries.text:
No, because Call to Battle requires the player to choose the move destination, so the restriction on valid destinations applies directly.

When a spell or ability has the player choose a move destination, that destination must be somewhere other than the unit's current location. [CR 355.4] [CR 355.4.a]

A play that cannot satisfy this requirement cannot be put onto the chain. [CR 355.8]

This contrasts with Flash, which specifies its destination — base — rather than requiring the player to choose one.
Because no destination choice is made when playing Flash, this restriction never applies, and a unit already in base is a valid target.

entries.question: How does Diana's ability work?
entries.text:
Diana's ability — "When a showdown begins here, you may pay 1 energy. If you do, Predict, then reveal the top card of your Main Deck. If it's a spell, draw it." — breaks into three distinct parts.

"When a showdown begins here" is the trigger condition.
It fires whenever a showdown begins at Diana's battlefield, whether that is a combat showdown or a non-combat showdown.

"you may" appears as the first part of the effect, so the controller chooses whether to place the triggered ability on the chain at all when the condition is met. [CR 383.3.a]
If you decline, the ability never goes on the chain and nothing happens.

"pay 1 energy. If you do, …" is resolution-time effect text.
"Pay 1 energy" is not a cost within instructions — those are identified by the "[do X] to [do Y]" template — so the ability has no cost at finalization. [CR 742.1]
Everything here executes when the ability resolves.
What happens with the payment depends on the state of your rune pool:

- If you have 1 or more Energy floating, it is consumed automatically.
You cannot prevent or decline this.
- If you have no floating Energy, you may activate Add reactions (exhaust runes or use other Add abilities) to generate it at this moment. [CR 429.3] [CR 429.3.a]
However, the game cannot compel you to do so.
You may choose not to activate any Add abilities and leave the payment unpaid.

The "If you do" conditional — Predict, then reveal the top card of your main deck — only applies if the Energy was paid, whether consumed from floating resources or generated via Add reactions.
If no Energy was paid, the remainder of the ability is skipped entirely.

entries.question: How does Emperor's Dais's ability work?
entries.text:
Emperor's Dais's ability — "When you conquer here, you may pay 1 energy and return a unit you control here to its owner's hand. If you do, play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token here." — breaks into three distinct parts.

"When you conquer here" is the trigger condition.
It fires when you establish control over Emperor's Dais at the end of a showdown.

"you may" appears as the first part of the effect, so you decide whether to place the triggered ability on the chain at all when the condition is met. [CR 383.3.a]
If you decline, nothing happens.

"pay 1 energy and return a unit you control here to its owner's hand. If you do, …" is resolution-time effect text.
"Pay 1 energy" is not a cost within instructions — those are identified by the "[do X] to [do Y]" template — so the ability has no cost at finalization. [CR 742.1]
However, "return a unit you control here" requires you to choose a target unit during finalization. [CR 402.1]
This choice is mandatory — if a legal target exists, you must choose one and cannot decline this step. [CR 402.3.b]

When the ability resolves, both instructions execute in sequence.
First, "pay 1 energy." What happens depends on the state of your rune pool:

- If you have 1 or more Energy floating, it is consumed automatically.
You cannot prevent or decline this.
- If you have no floating Energy, you may activate Add reactions (exhaust runes or use other Add abilities) to generate it at this moment. [CR 429.3] [CR 429.3.a]
However, the game cannot compel you to do so.
You may choose not to activate any Add abilities and leave the payment unpaid.

Second, "return a unit you control here to its owner's hand" — the targeted unit is returned regardless of whether the Energy was paid. [CR 055]
If the unit has left the battlefield before the ability resolves, it is not returned. [CR 405.1]

The "If you do" conditional — play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token here — only applies if both the Energy was paid and the unit was successfully returned.
If either fails, no Sand Soldier is played.

entries.question: Can Flash target a unit that is already in base?

Impossible instructions are ignored, and everything else resolves normally. [CR 055]

entries.question: How does Gangplank's replacement effect interact with Switcheroo?
entries.text:
Only the modifier applied to Gangplank is a candidate for replacement — whatever happens to the other unit is untouched.
See How does Switcheroo work? for why Swapping creates two separate modifiers from a single calculated difference. [CR 433.1.a] [CR 433.1.b]
Whichever of the two modifiers chooses Gangplank is the only one his replacement effect can apply to — if it's a decrease, it's replaced with +3 might instead; if it's an increase, it isn't one of the events his ability replaces, so it applies normally.
Either way, the other unit's modifier resolves untouched, and the difference itself isn't recalculated afterward.

 Gangplank's replacement effect intercedes on his -5 might modifier — decreasing his might is one of the events it replaces — and turns it into +3 might instead.
 Determined Sentry's +5 might modifier never chose Gangplank, so it's unaffected.

 Gangplank ends at 9 might (6 base + 3); Determined Sentry ends at 6 might (1 base + 5).

Additional costs — such as the optional Accelerate cost — are applied in a separate step after the base cost is zeroed out and are unaffected by the "ignoring its cost" instruction. [CR 356.1.b.3]

entries.question: If I play Irresistible Faefolk directly to a battlefield, does its ability trigger?
entries.text:
No — playing a unit to a battlefield is not a move, so the ability does not trigger.

A move is defined as a permanent changing its position from one location on the board to another. [CR 441.1]
Playing a card involves it entering the board from a non-board zone (such as your hand), which is a zone change, not a move. [CR 441.2]
Because Irresistible Faefolk's ability specifically triggers when it moves to a battlefield, playing it directly there does not satisfy that trigger condition.

entries.question: If an opponent responds to my move trigger by removing Irresistible Faefolk from the battlefield, does the enemy unit still move?
entries.text:
Yes — the enemy unit still moves to that battlefield.

Irresistible Faefolk's trigger condition is moving to a battlefield, and "that battlefield" in the effect is a referent to the battlefield named in that trigger condition.
Information referenced from a trigger condition is checked when the trigger condition is fulfilled, not when the ability resolves. [CR 359.3.f.3]
That means "that battlefield" was already fixed the moment Irresistible Faefolk moved there and placed the ability on the chain.

Suppose an opponent responds to the triggered ability by playing Gust (or similarly, Star-Crossed), targeting Irresistible Faefolk itself to return it to your hand.
Irresistible Faefolk returns to your hand, but the triggered ability is unaffected — it's already an independent item on the chain, and the battlefield it references was fixed at trigger time.
When it resolves, it moves an enemy unit to that battlefield, even though Irresistible Faefolk is no longer there.

This is different from referents like "here," "my," or "its," which are checked when the instruction resolves rather than when the trigger condition is met — those can mistarget if the relevant game object or location is no longer valid at that time. [CR 359.3.f.2]

entries.question: If I move Irresistible Faefolk to an open battlefield and pull an enemy unit there, who is the attacker?
entries.text:
You — the Irresistible Faefolk player — are the attacker.

When Irresistible Faefolk moves to an open (uncontrolled) battlefield, that move applies the contested status to the battlefield. [CR 445] [CR 187.3.a]
During the cleanup that follows the move, a combat is staged because units from opposing players are now present at the contested battlefield. [CR 323.9]
When combat opens, the attacker is defined as the player whose unit(s) applied the contested status. [CR 459.2.b.1]
That is you — the player who moved Irresistible Faefolk.
The opponent whose unit was pulled in is the defender. [CR 459.2.b.2]

entries.question: Does Karthus's ability apply if he dies from the same effect as the unit with Deathknell?
entries.text:
Yes, because Deathknell triggers are always queued as pending items before the dying unit leaves the board.

Whenever a unit with Deathknell is killed — whether by a Kill effect or by damage during a cleanup — its trigger is added to the chain before the card is moved to the trash. [CR 808.1.d.2]
Karthus's passive is only active while he is on the board, [CR 365.1] but because the trigger is queued first, he is still present when it is added — even if he is dying from the same effect.
In the cleanup case this ordering is enforced explicitly: step 3a queues all Deathknell triggers [CR 323.4] before step 3b moves any of those units to the trash. [CR 323.5]

entries.question: Does a single Not So Fast counter both Deathknell triggers when Karthus is on the board?
entries.text:
No — Karthus places two separate trigger instances on the chain, and Not So Fast can only counter one of them at a time.

When a friendly unit with Deathknell dies while Karthus is on the board, his ability causes that Deathknell to trigger an additional time.
Each trigger is added to the chain as its own independent pending item. [CR 808.1.d.2]
Not So Fast counters a single spell or ability, so one copy intercepts only one of the two triggers; the other resolves normally.
Stopping both requires two copies of Not So Fast.

entries.question: Can an opponent play a unit in reaction to Kha'Zix's trigger to prevent the effect?
entries.text:
No.
Once Kha'Zix's ability is on the chain, adding more units cannot prevent it from resolving.

Kha'Zix's ability reads "When I attack or defend, if an enemy unit is alone here, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP."
The "if" clause immediately follows the trigger condition, making it an intervening if. [CR 383.3.e]
This means the condition is evaluated exactly once — at the moment Kha'Zix gains the attacker or defender designation — and must be true at that moment for the ability to be placed on the chain at all. [CR 383.4.e.2.b] [CR 383.4.f.2.b]

If the enemy unit is alone when that designation is gained, the ability goes on the chain immediately.
The condition is not re-evaluated on resolution, so an opponent playing an additional unit as a reaction cannot remove the ability from the chain or prevent Kha'Zix from gaining the +2 Might and the 2 XP.

Note also that the reverse is true: if a second enemy unit is already present when Kha'Zix gains its designation, the condition fails and the ability is never placed on the chain, even if that second unit is later removed.

callouts.title: Contrast: if the condition were at the end
callouts.text:
If Kha'Zix instead read "When I attack or defend, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP if an enemy unit is alone here," the "if" clause would come after the effect instruction rather than immediately after the trigger condition.
 In that case the "if" would be part of the effect rather than the trigger condition, so it would not be an intervening if: the ability would go on the chain whenever Kha'Zix attacks or defends, regardless of whether an enemy unit is alone, and the condition would only be evaluated when it resolves.
 An opponent could then play a unit at reaction speed to ensure two units are present at resolution, preventing the +2 Might and the 2 XP.

entries.question: Can Kha'Zix trigger multiple times in the same turn?
entries.text:
Yes.
The once-per-combat limit on attack and defend triggers applies to each combat individually, not to the entire turn, so Kha'Zix can gain +2 Might and 2 XP once in each separate combat it participates in. [CR 383.4.e.2.a] [CR 383.4.f.2.a]

Each time Kha'Zix enters a new combat it gains its attacker or defender designation for the first time in that combat, which is what triggers the ability.
There is no rule preventing a unit from participating in multiple combats per turn, and each combat is an independent instance with its own once-per-combat tracking.

For more on how attack and defend triggers work per combat, see When do attack/defend triggers happen?.

callouts.text:
After Kha'Zix wins a combat and the state returns to neutral open, you can play Charm to pull a different enemy unit onto Kha'Zix's battlefield.
 That unit becoming present at a battlefield Kha'Zix's controller already controls applies contested status, staging a new, distinct combat.
 When that combat opens, Kha'Zix gains the defender designation for the first time in that combat.
 If the pulled unit is alone, the intervening-if condition is satisfied and Kha'Zix triggers again.
 Playing additional Charms repeats this cycle for as long as enemy units and Charms are available.

entries.question: Can Lacerate target a unit that doesn't have 3 might or less?
entries.text:
Yes, Lacerate can target any unit, regardless of its might.

"Choose a unit" targets a unit, [CR 355.7] [CR 355.9.a] and that choice carries no targeting restriction at all — "unit" only identifies the category of game object being targeted, not a restriction on it. [CR 355.9.a.1]
The instruction to kill it "if it has 3 might or less" is not part of the target description at all — it's a condition checked on the effect itself as Lacerate resolves.
This is unlike a card such as Gust, which reads "Return a unit at a battlefield with 3 might or less to its owner's hand" — there, "with 3 might or less" describes the target, so it's a genuine targeting restriction and only such units are valid choices. [CR 359.3.e.4]

entries.question: If my opponent targets my spell with Lilting Lullaby and I counter my own spell in response, can I still play spells?
entries.text:
Yes.
Countering your own spell removes it from the chain, so Lilting Lullaby has no valid target when it resolves — and with nothing to counter, the linked restriction on playing spells is also ignored.

When you counter your own spell, it is cleared from the chain. [CR 425.1.a]
"Spell" in a targeting context refers to objects on the chain. [CR 355.9.a.2]
By the time Lilting Lullaby resolves, its target is no longer on the chain and no longer meets the targeting requirements — this is mistargeting. [CR 359.3.e.2] [CR 359.3.e.9]

Because all of Lilting Lullaby's first instruction's targets are now invalid, the "Counter a spell" instruction does not execute. [CR 359.3.e.7]

"Counter a spell" and "Its controller can't play spells this turn" are linked instructions — the second references the controller of the spell from the first.
Since the earlier linked instruction was ignored, the later one is ignored as well. [CR 359.3.e.14.a]

entries.question: Does Lotus Trap affect how much damage needs to be assigned in combat?
entries.text:
No.
Assignment and dealing are separate steps in the combat sequence, and Lotus Trap only applies at the dealing step.

Lotus Trap is a replacement effect that applies when damage is dealt, not when it is assigned.
The combat damage sequence treats these as two separate and distinct steps. [CR 460.2.c.1] [CR 460.2.c.1.a]

The assignment step requires lethal damage to be assigned to a unit in full before any remaining damage may be assigned to a different unit. [CR 460.2.c.3]
Lethal damage is defined as non-zero damage equalling or exceeding a unit's might — this definition makes no reference to replacement effects that apply at the time of dealing.
Lotus Trap's doubling only becomes relevant later, when damage is actually dealt. [CR 460.2.d]

entries.question: Does Burn or Minefield trigger Nocturne's ability?
entries.text:
No — Burn only puts cards into your trash; it never looks at or reveals anything, and Nocturne's ability only cares about those two specific actions.
Minefield's printed ability works the same way, and this won't change even if its wording is later updated to explicitly read Burn 2.

Nocturne's ability reads "As you look at or reveal me from the top of your deck, you may banish me. If you do, you may play me for Universal."
That phrasing ties the permission to the specific action of looking at or revealing Nocturne — the same construction the rules use elsewhere to key an effect to one exact moment rather than a general state, such as choices made "As I am played." [CR 355.1]

Reveal is a defined action, and a player may only reveal cards when a game effect specifically instructs them to. [CR 424.1] [CR 424.2] [CR 424.2.a]
"Look" doesn't have its own numbered definition yet, but it's treated the same way — the main deck is secret information specifically because it "cannot be looked through or revealed unless instructed by a card effect." [CR 103.2.e] [CR 103.2.e.1]

Burn does neither of these — it puts cards from the top of your main deck directly into your trash, with no instruction to look at or reveal them. [CR 431.1.b]
Minefield's printed ability, "When you conquer here, put the top 2 cards of your Main Deck into your trash," does exactly the same thing — it's already functionally identical to Burn 2, so an errata formalizing it as such wouldn't add a look or reveal instruction that isn't already there.
Either way, those cards only become visible because they land in the trash, a public zone by default, [CR 108.2.d] not because anyone looked at or revealed them first.

Since neither instructs anyone to look at or reveal Nocturne, its ability is never triggered by Burn or by Minefield.

callouts.text:
"Look" is not yet defined as its own numbered action the way "reveal" is.
 The core rules consistently treat it as a parallel, explicitly-instructed action alongside reveal wherever both are mentioned, and this ruling relies on that pattern — an official update giving "look" its own definition would let this be cited directly.

entries.question: Can Ruined Rex's Deathknell target the Mech tokens created by Ferrous Forerunner's Deathknell, if both die at the same time?
entries.text:
No.
Targets are chosen during finalization, and Ferrous Forerunner's Mech tokens are not created until its Deathknell resolves — which only happens after all pending items have been finalized.

When both units die in the same cleanup, their Deathknell triggers are queued as pending items simultaneously in turn order, [CR 323.4] [CR 383.3.d.1] and items finalize in the order they were appended. [CR 337.1.b]
No item resolves until all pending items have been finalized. [CR 337.1.c.3]

If Ferrous Forerunner's controller is the turn player, their trigger is queued first and finalizes first.
The ability does not resolve yet and no Mech tokens are created.
When Ruined Rex's trigger then finalizes and must choose a target, [CR 355.5] Ferrous Forerunner's ability still has not resolved, so the Mechs do not yet exist on the board.

If Ruined Rex's controller is the turn player, Rex's trigger is queued first and finalizes first.
It must choose a target immediately [CR 355.5] — before Ferrous Forerunner's trigger has even finalized, let alone resolved.
Again, no Mechs exist.

Either way, once Ruined Rex's trigger has finalized, its target choice is locked in and cannot be changed. [CR 355.15]

entries.question: Does Ruined Rex's Deathknell deal damage before or after units are healed at the end of combat?
entries.text:
After.
The combat heal is part of the same cleanup that queues the trigger, and the trigger does not resolve until that cleanup has run to completion.

When Ruined Rex dies with lethal damage during a combat cleanup, the steps run in this order:

1. Step 3a — Ruined Rex's Deathknell trigger is added to the chain as a pending item. [CR 323.4] [CR 808.1.d.2]
2. Step 3b — Ruined Rex is moved to the trash. [CR 323.5]
3. Step 3c — All units are healed. This step is inserted by the combat special cleanup. [CR 461.1.a.1]

The pending trigger does not begin finalization until the cleanup task is complete. [CR 335]
Only then does it enter the FEPR process, get finalized (targets chosen), and resolve — dealing 4 damage to the chosen enemy unit.

entries.question: If Sacrifice is countered, is the killed unit returned?
entries.text:
No, as the kill is an additional cost and countering a spell never refunds costs already paid.

Killing a friendly Mighty unit is an additional cost required to play Sacrifice.
A countered spell does nothing and is not considered to have been played. [CR 425.1.a] [CR 425.1.b]
Countering does not refund any costs paid to play a card, including additional costs. [CR 425.1.c] [CR 425.1.c.1]
That cost is paid before the spell resolves, so the killed unit is not returned.

entries.question: Does the Deathknell of the unit killed as the cost resolve before Sacrifice draws and channels?
entries.text:
Yes.
The kill is a non-standard additional cost, not a resolution instruction, so it happens during finalization.
That puts the Deathknell on top of Sacrifice on the chain, where it resolves first.

The opening line of Sacrifice — "as an additional cost to play this, kill a friendly Mighty unit" — is a cost, not a line of rules text that executes on resolution. [CR 356.6]
Costs are paid in step 4 of the play process, before Sacrifice has even finished being finalized. [CR 357.2]

When a unit with Deathknell is killed to pay that cost in step 4, its Deathknell ability is added to the chain as a pending item before the unit moves to the trash. [CR 428.1.a.1.b] [CR 808.1.d.2]
At this point the chain holds two pending items: the Deathknell above, and Sacrifice below, still mid-finalization.

Sacrifice then continues through step 5 (legality check) and step 6, becoming a finalized chain item. [CR 359.3.a]
Because the Deathknell is still a pending item at that point, it completes its own finalization steps before play proceeds. [CR 359.3.b]

Once both items are finalized, the chain resolves from the top down.
The Deathknell was added last, sits on top, and resolves first.
Only after it fully resolves does Sacrifice resolve — drawing 2 and channeling 1 rune exhausted.

callouts.text:
You kill Rift Herald, whose Deathknell reads "Play a unit from your hand to your base, ignoring its Energy cost," to pay Sacrifice's cost.
 The Deathknell resolves first — you play a free unit from your pre-draw hand — then Sacrifice resolves and you draw 2 and channel 1 rune exhausted.

entries.question: Can my opponent interact before the chosen Mighty unit is killed?
entries.text:
No.
The unit is not a target, and finalization does not pass priority, leaving no window to react to either the choice or the kill.

The unit killed as a cost is not a target — objects referenced as part of a cost are explicitly excluded from targeting. [CR 355.10.c]

Costs are paid during step 4 of finalization, and finalization does not pass priority. [CR 357.2] [CR 337.1.a]
An opponent cannot play a spell like Stupefy — which reads "Give a unit -1 Might this turn, to a minimum of 1 Might" — to reduce the unit's Might and make it no longer Mighty before the cost is paid.
The first opportunity for either player to act is after Sacrifice is fully finalized, by which point the cost has already been paid and the unit is already in the trash.

entries.question: Does a Reflection token with Temporary lose Temporary after Shady Spectacles makes it a copy of a unit that doesn't have Temporary?
entries.text:
No — it keeps Temporary, no matter what it becomes a copy of.

Shady Spectacles' "becomes a copy of that unit" is a copy effect, and copy effects apply in the trait-altering layer — the first of the layers used to resolve continuous effects. [CR 472] [CR 472.1] [CR 472.1.b] This layer replaces the equipped unit's traits and rules text with the chosen unit's. [CR 472.1.b.1]

The copied unit not having Temporary doesn't matter — copying it doesn't strip Temporary from the token, because the two effects operate in different layers. Granting a keyword like Temporary happens in the ability-altering layer, applied right after the trait-altering layer. [CR 472.2] [CR 472.2.a] A Reflection token's Temporary comes from a separate effect — Deceiver's conquer-or-hold ability or Mirror Image's effect — that already applied when the token was created, before Shady Spectacles ever attaches. Since that grant sits in a different layer, Shady Spectacles' copy effect has no say over it, and it keeps applying no matter what the token becomes a copy of.

entries.question: How does Smite interact with death-saving effects like Guardian Angel, Zhonya's Hourglass, or Tactical Retreat?
entries.text:
Death-saving effects can prevent the banish, because the unit's owner decides which replacement effect applies first and can apply their protective effect before Smite's.

Smite's "if it would die this turn, banish it instead" is a replacement effect. [CR 369.1]
So are each of the three protective effects, which all replace the event of a unit dying.
When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the owner of the affected unit decides the order they apply. [CR 372]

If the unit's owner applies their protective effect first, the death event is fully replaced — the unit is healed, exhausted, and recalled, or an equipment dies in its place.
A replacement effect can only be applied once to an event, and to any events that replace it; [CR 370.2] once the death event has been consumed, Smite's replacement effect has no qualifying event left to intercept, and the unit is not banished.

Conversely, if Smite's effect is applied first, the unit is banished.
The protective effects each replace a "die" event — since banishment is not a subset of dying, [CR 427.2.a] none of them can chain onto the resulting "banish" event.
That said, a unit's owner would never choose this order if their intent is to save it, so Smite effectively cannot banish a unit that has a death-saving effect protecting it.

entries.question: How does Switcheroo work?
entries.text:
Switcheroo does not swap might values directly — it determines the difference in current might at resolution and applies +X/-X modifiers accordingly.

Switcheroo uses the Swap action, [CR 433] which calculates the difference between the two units' current might, then applies a -X modifier to the higher might unit and a +X modifier to the lower might unit.
Current might means the unit's total might at resolution time, including all active modifiers: equipment bonuses, battlefield passives, conditional abilities, and any other effects.
The modifiers Switcheroo applies persist until end of turn.

Each modifier is independent: when equipment detaches or a passive deactivates, only that specific bonus is removed; the Switcheroo modifier remains until end of turn.

entries.question: Can Switcheroo result in negative might?
entries.text:
Yes, but the unit treats its might as 0 for game purposes while calculations still use the actual negative value.

Units can end up with negative might when modifiers included in their current might at resolution are later removed.
Units with might less than 0 are treated as having 0 might when referenced by spells and abilities, and when summing might to be assigned as damage in the Combat Damage Step. [CR 143.2.b]
Units with 0 or negative might do not automatically die — units are only killed during cleanup if they have non-zero damage equal to or exceeding their might. [CR 323.5]

If a unit later gains additional might modifiers, they add to the actual negative value.

 The unit ends up with 3 might — the +5 modifier adds to the actual -2 value.

entries.question: Can I banish my only unit at a battlefield I control and replay it there without losing control in between?
entries.text:
Yes, control of the battlefield is never lost during this sequence.

When Temporal Breach resolves, the replayed unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [CR 354.2] with its play process held until the spell has fully resolved. [CR 354.3]
Once the spell finishes resolving, a cleanup runs — but the pending unit keeps the chain alive throughout it.
Because the chain is not empty, the turn remains in a closed state, and cleanup step 4 — which would make the battlefield uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [CR 323.6]
Control is never lost, so any effects that care about gaining or losing control of that battlefield don't trigger.
When all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized [CR 335.2] and replayed to the same battlefield you still control, as dictated by Temporal Breach's own text.

entries.question: Can Temporal Breach banish a unit at a different battlefield if played from Hidden?
entries.text:
No, when Temporal Breach is played from Hidden, the unit it banishes must be chosen from among units at the battlefield where it was hidden.

"Banish a unit" chooses a specific game object to affect, making it a target, declared as Temporal Breach is put on the chain. [CR 355.5] [CR 355.7] [CR 355.8]
Choices made while playing a card from Hidden are restricted to the battlefield where it was hidden. [CR 811.1.d]
Specifically, if a Hidden spell chooses any targets, those targets must be chosen from among options at that battlefield, unless the ability explicitly restricts targeting in a way that makes this impossible. [CR 811.1.d.2]
Temporal Breach's own wording doesn't restrict its target to a location, so this Hidden restriction applies in full — a unit at another battlefield, or in base, isn't a legal target when it's played from Hidden.

If Temporal Breach is instead played normally — paying its cost rather than from its facedown state — none of this applies, and it can target any unit anywhere with no restrictions on targeting. [CR 811.3]

entries.question: Can I pay optional additional costs, like Accelerate, when replaying the banished unit?
entries.text:
Yes, since the replayed unit still goes through the complete, normal process of playing a card, and "ignoring its cost" only narrows one part of that process — the base cost — leaving everything else, including optional additional costs, unaffected.

"Its owner plays it" instructs the normal process of playing a card — the unit is removed from banishment and put onto the chain as a pending item, [CR 354] [CR 354.2] it isn't placed directly onto the board.
That pending item goes through the full finalization process once it's ready to be finalized, including making relevant choices [CR 355] and determining total cost. [CR 356]
Playing a card "ignoring its cost" only sets its base Energy and base Power cost to zero; [CR 356.1.b.1] further additional costs applied in later steps can still raise the total cost back above zero. [CR 356.1.b.3]
Accelerate is one such optional additional cost, paid as a player plays the unit with the ability, [CR 805.2] so its owner may still declare their intent to pay it during finalization [CR 356.2.b.1] and pay it as usual, unaffected by Temporal Breach ignoring the unit's base cost.

entries.question: What happens if Temporal Breach banishes a unit at Rockfall Path?
entries.text:
Temporal Breach still resolves fully, but the unit is never actually replayed — it stays in its owner's banishment for the rest of the game, since Rockfall Path reads "Units can't be played here" and Temporal Breach forces the unit back to that exact battlefield with no alternative.

"Then its owner plays it to the same location" only adds the unit to the chain as a pending item — it doesn't check whether the destination is legal, so Temporal Breach's own resolution is unaffected by Rockfall Path's restriction. [CR 354.2]
The unit only runs into trouble once it's finalized on its own, since checking legality at that point catches units being played to a battlefield where that's forbidden. [CR 358.2]
Because Temporal Breach fixes the destination with no alternative, that check can never pass, so the finalization attempt is undone and the unit returns to the banishment it was played from [CR 358.4] — for good.

The step-by-step below spells this out.

### Resolution Sequence

1. Temporal Breach resolves. "Banish a unit" banishes the targeted unit, which was at Rockfall Path.
2. "Then its owner plays it to the same location, ignoring its cost" removes the unit from banishment and adds it to the chain as a pending item. [CR 354.2]
3. Temporal Breach finishes resolving.
4. Once all outstanding tasks are complete, the unit is ready to be finalized and goes through steps 2 through 5 of playing a card on its own. [CR 359.3.b] Its location is fixed as Rockfall Path by Temporal Breach's own text.
5. At step 5 ("Check Legality"), playing the unit to Rockfall Path would create an illegal state, since Rockfall Path prevents units from being played there. [CR 358.2]
6. The actions taken while playing the unit are undone and the action is cancelled. [CR 358.4] That undoes step 2's removal of the unit from banishment, [CR 354] so the unit returns there — and stays there for the rest of the game.

entries.question: Does Vex's triggered ability target the unit that was just played?
entries.text:
No, as the unit to be stunned is determined automatically, so no targeting ever occurs.

Because no choice is ever made about which unit is stunned, the unit is not a target. [CR 355.10.d]

This means targeting protection — such as "I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" — offers no defense against the stun.

2. Apply cost increases: [CR 356.3] Vex's ability increases enemy spell costs by 1 energyUniversal. This is applied to the total cost even though the base cost is zero

entries.question: When do I pay costs within instructions using "may"?
entries.text:
At finalization — when placing the triggered ability on the chain.

In rules text phrased as "[do X] to [do Y]," the [do X] part is considered a cost within instructions.
For triggered abilities, this cost is treated as the base cost of the ability and must be paid in order to finalize it to the chain. [CR 383.3.b] [CR 383.3.b.1] [CR 742.1.b] [CR 403.1.b.1]
If the controller declines to pay, the ability is not placed on the chain at all.

 At finalization, the controller must decide whether to pay the 1 energy cost.
 If they decline, the ability is not placed on the chain.
 If they pay, the ability goes on the chain and opponents have the opportunity to react before it resolves.

entries.question: How are additional conditions in triggered abilities evaluated?
entries.text:
It depends on where the condition appears in the ability's text.

In Riftbound, the trigger condition is precisely the event that follows "When", "At", or "The [Nth] time" — including any qualifiers on that event, up to the first comma. [CR 383.2.a]
Everything after that comma is the ability's effect. [CR 383.2.b]

Conditions before the comma are part of the trigger condition and must be satisfied for the ability to be placed on the chain at all.
For example, Sunken Temple reads "When you conquer here with one or more Mighty units, you may pay 1 energy to draw 1."
The requirement that the conquering units be Mighty is embedded in the trigger condition; if no Mighty unit participated in the conquer, the ability does not trigger.

"If" clauses that immediately follow the trigger condition — as the first thing after the comma — are checked at trigger time.
This is the "intervening if rule": if the condition is not satisfied at the moment the triggering event occurs, the ability is never placed on the chain at all. [CR 383.3.e]

However, "if" clauses embedded within the effect text — coming after an effect instruction rather than immediately after the comma — are only checked on resolution.
The ability goes on the chain regardless, and the condition is only evaluated when it resolves.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
Gutter Palace reads "At the start of your Beginning Phase, if you have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields, you win the game."

 The "if" clause comes immediately after the comma, so it is an intervening if.
 This ability is only placed on the chain if you already have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields at the start of your Beginning Phase.
 If the condition is not satisfied at that moment, the ability does not trigger at all.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
Loose Cannon reads "At start of your Beginning Phase, draw 1 if you have one or fewer cards in your hand."

 Here the "if" clause does not immediately follow the comma — it comes after the effect instruction "draw 1".
 This means it is not an intervening if.
 The ability goes on the chain at the start of every one of your Beginning Phases, regardless of how many cards are in your hand.
 Only when the ability resolves is the hand size checked; if you have more than one card at that point, the draw does not happen.

review.evidence: The controlling 2026-04-29 clarification explicitly replaces the first-comma model with a structured sequence for adjacent conditions, choices, and costs; this answer teaches the superseded model.

entries.question: When do triggered abilities trigger?
entries.text:
When their condition is met, triggered abilities go on the chain immediately, regardless of whose turn it is. [CR 383.3] [CR 383.3.c]

The Reaction keyword is not required for this to work on an opponent's turn.
Unlike spells and activated abilities which require Reaction to be played outside your turn, triggered abilities are automatic and will trigger whenever their condition is met, on any player's turn.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
Blade Dancer triggers when you choose a friendly unit.
 This can happen on your opponent's turn, for example when you play a Reaction spell that targets one of your own units.

entries.question: Can I react to units being played?
entries.text:
No, as units enter the board immediately without priority being passed to other players.

Unlike spells, units resolve the moment they are finalized and do not open a window of opportunity for reactions — they enter the board immediately without priority being passed to other players. [CR 337.1.c] [CR 359.2]

If the unit has a play effect ("When you play me…"), or if another permanent's triggered ability fires as it enters the board, those triggered abilities are placed on the chain as pending items after the unit has already entered. [CR 383.4.a.2] [CR 383.3]
Once those pending items are finalized with no further items pending, priority passes and players may react [CR 337.1.c.3] — but by that point, the unit is already in play.

entries.question: Can I play a reaction after one, but not all, items on the chain have resolved?
entries.text:
Yes, once you have gained priority.
The chain does not have to resolve in its entirety prior to (re)gaining priority, unlike in some other TCGs.

Any time the most recent item on the chain resolves and there are no pending items, the controller of the newest item on the chain gains priority. [CR 337.1.c.3] [CR 340.4]

callouts.text:
You put Singularity on the chain targeting an opponent's unit.
 Your opponent reacts by putting their Wind Wall on the chain, attempting to counter the Singularity.
 In response, you play Stupefy, in the hopes of drawing into a counterspell of your own.
 Once Stupefy resolves and you draw a card, priority is back to your opponent as the most recent item is their Wind Wall.
 After they pass priority, you can react once again and play your own counterspell, assuming you drew it off of the Stupefy.

entries.question: When do attack/defend triggers happen?
entries.text:
Attack and defend triggered abilities (such as "When I attack" or "When I defend") trigger when a unit receives its attacker or defender designation, not necessarily at the start of combat.
These designations are assigned during cleanups, [CR 323.2] which means units don't need to be present at the beginning of combat to get their triggers.

### Units can join combat late and still trigger

If a unit is moved into a battlefield where combat is already in progress, it will receive the appropriate attacker or defender designation during the next cleanup. [CR 323.2.a]
When it receives this designation, any "When I attack" or "When I defend" abilities will trigger at that time.

### Attack/Defend abilities only trigger once per combat

Attack and defend triggered abilities can only trigger once per combat, even if a unit gains and loses its designation multiple times. [CR 383.4.e.2.a] [CR 383.4.f.2.a]

Once a unit has been assigned an attacker or defender designation during a combat, moving it away from the battlefield will cause it to lose that designation. [CR 323.2.c]
If that unit is moved back to the same battlefield during the same combat, it will gain the same designation as its controller, [CR 323.2.a] which will be the same designation it previously had.
However, its "When I attack" or "When I defend" ability will not trigger again, as these abilities can only be fulfilled once per combat.

entries.question: What happens when I move a unit into a non-combat showdown?
entries.text:
When a unit controlled by a different player becomes present at the battlefield during a non-combat showdown, the showdown immediately converts into a combat showdown. [CR 316.5.b.1.a]
This conversion happens during the cleanup at the end of the action that caused the unit to arrive. [CR 323.14]

Once converted to a combat showdown, combat-related keywords (such as Assault or Shield) take effect, attacker and defender designations are assigned during the next cleanup, [CR 323.2] and attack or defend triggers can happen.
The player who originally applied contested status to the battlefield becomes the attacker, [CR 459.2.b.1] and the player who moved in during the showdown becomes the defender — a scenario the community calls the surprise defender.

entries.question: When does a showdown close?

entries.question: Does "you may" mean I choose the target at resolution?
entries.text:
No, as targets must always be declared when putting a spell or ability on the chain, not at resolution.

Targets are always declared when putting a spell or ability on the chain, [CR 355.8] not at resolution.
If a "you may" effect involves choosing a game object, that choice is still a target and must be declared upfront.
The "you may" means the effect or ability is optional — you can decline to complete it on resolution — but it does not defer when the target is declared.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
Disarming Rake reads "When you play me, you may kill a gear."

 When this triggered ability is put on the chain, you must immediately declare the gear to kill as a target.
 You cannot wait until resolution to decide which gear to name, and you cannot put the ability on the chain without a valid gear target at all.

 The "you may" only means you can decline to complete the kill when the ability resolves — it does not make the gear target optional.

entries.question: What makes something a target?
entries.text:
Any game object, player, or zone that a spell or ability chooses to affect is a target, [CR 355.7] and must be declared when putting that spell or ability on the chain. [CR 355.8]

Card text rarely uses the word "target" or "choose" explicitly — most of the time targeting is implied, as in "Kill a unit" or "Move a friendly unit."
Abilities that reference "when you choose" a game object, such as Irelia, Fervent's "When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn," are specifically triggered when being targeted.

When in doubt, assume it is a target — the list below covers the only situations where it is not:

- It is in a private zone (hand, deck, etc.) [CR 355.10.a] e.g., "You may play a unit from your hand" does not target a unit — it merely lets you play one.
- It is only a location requirement for another target. [CR 355.10.b] Words like "at a battlefield" narrow down which objects are valid targets; the battlefield itself is not a target — unless the effect lets you choose which of several battlefields to affect, as in "Kill all units at a battlefield."
- It is part of a trigger condition, cost, or replacement effect. [CR 355.10.c] [CR 355.10.c.1] Objects referenced in "when X happens" conditions, payment costs (see also When do I pay costs within instructions using "may"?), or "instead" effects are not targets. e.g., the dying unit in "When a friendly unit dies, kill a gear" is not a target — only the gear is.
- There is no real choice involved. [CR 355.10.d] If an effect applies to every object meeting a description rather than a specific one you pick, nothing is targeted. e.g., "Kill all units at battlefields" targets nothing because you are not choosing among individual units.
- Another player makes the choice. [CR 355.10.e] Targeting requires that you make the choice. e.g., "Each player kills a unit they control" does not target — each player picks their own unit when the spell resolves.
- The instruction uses "must". [CR 355.10.f] This signals the choice is made on resolution rather than upfront. e.g., "You must recycle one of your runes" does not target, whereas "Recycle a rune you control" does.

entries.question: Can I use Ambush to play a unit to my base?
entries.text:
No.
Ambush only permits playing a unit to a battlefield; it has no effect on your base.

Ambush is shorthand for "I may be played to a battlefield where you control units" and "I have Reaction as long as I'm being played to a battlefield where you control units." [CR 822.1.b]
The permission Ambush grants is strictly limited to battlefields — a base is not a battlefield, so Ambush never makes it a valid destination. [CR 822.1.c]
Playing a unit to your base is already permitted by the default rules for valid locations [CR 355.2.a] and carries no timing restriction — the distinctive benefit Ambush provides is Reaction, but that only applies when playing to a battlefield.

entries.question: Can opponents react to a unit being played with Ambush?
entries.text:
No.
Ambush grants the unit Reaction speed, which determines when it can be played — it does not create a window for opponents to respond before the unit enters.

Units resolve the moment they are finalized without entering the Execute step, [CR 337.1.c] and finalization does not pass priority. [CR 337.1.a]
The unit enters the board immediately, just as any unit played during an Open State would (see also Can I react to units being played?).

This is a common point of confusion with cards like Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror, which has Ambush and triggers if an enemy unit is alone when he attacks or defends.
An opponent cannot play a unit in response to Kha'Zix being placed on the chain in an attempt to break the "alone" condition before he enters.

entries.question: Who gets to act after I Ambush a unit during a showdown?
entries.text:
It depends on whether anything else remains on the chain once the unit enters.

When played onto an empty chain, the unit enters immediately, the chain empties, and the turn returns to a Showdown Open State — focus passes to the next player in turn order. [CR 337.1.c.1.a]
This catches many players off guard — you move in to attack, Ambush a unit, and expect to retain focus, but your opponent gets to act first.

When played in response to something already on the chain — such as attack or defend triggers, or a spell — the turn does not return to an Open State after the unit resolves, so focus does not pass. [CR 346]
Priority instead passes to the controller of the newest remaining item on the chain. [CR 337.1.c.3]

entries.question: Which equipment effects choose units?
entries.text:
Equip and Quick Draw choose units; Weaponmaster does not.

Some abilities trigger or care about when you choose friendly units. Here's how equipment-related effects interact with such abilities:

- When you activate a gear's Equip ability, you choose a unit you control to attach the equipment to. [CR 818.1.b]
This choice is a target, so activating Equip counts as choosing a unit.
- When you play a gear with Quick Draw, its triggered ability instructs you to "attach it to a Unit you control". [CR 819.1.d]
While attaching cards doesn't inherently choose or specify a target, [CR 434.3] Quick Draw's ability does require you to choose which unit to attach to.
This counts as choosing a unit.
- When you play a unit with Weaponmaster, you choose an equipment you control, not the unit. [CR 821.1.c]
The rules explicitly state that "The Equip ability is not activated this way, and the unit with the Weaponmaster ability is not chosen". [CR 821.1.c.6]
Therefore, Weaponmaster does not count as choosing a unit.

entries.question: Can I react to equipment abilities?
entries.text:
Yes — all three equipment abilities create chain items that opponents can respond to before the attachment resolves.

Equip is an activated ability. [CR 818.1]
Activated abilities use the chain, [CR 377.3] so when you activate Equip, opponents have an opportunity to play a Reaction spell or ability before the attachment resolves. [CR 377.3.b.2]

When you play a Quick Draw gear, the gear itself resolves immediately when finalized and cannot be reacted to. [CR 337.1.c]
However, Quick Draw's triggered ability — "When you play this, attach it to a unit you control" [CR 819.1.d] — is placed on the chain as a separate item. [CR 383.3]
Opponents can respond to that ability before the attachment resolves.

Weaponmaster is also a triggered ability keyword. [CR 821.1]
Its ability triggers when you play the unit, and is placed on the chain just like any other triggered ability. [CR 383.3]
Opponents can respond to it before the equipment is attached.

Skipping straight to attaching without checking for reactions is not correct play for any of these abilities.

entries.question: What happens to attached equipment when you take control of an enemy unit?
entries.text:
Equipment stays attached but its controller does not change - only the top-most unit's controller changes.

When you take control of a unit, any equipment attached to it remains controlled by whoever originally controlled it.
Changes in control of the top-most card do not affect control of attached cards, and vice versa. [CR 718.5.f]

When the equipment detaches, it remains at the unit's last location. [CR 719.5] [CR 435.4.b]
If that location is a battlefield, it is recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [CR 435.4.a]
If that location is your base, it cannot remain there since other players cannot have game objects they control in another player's base, [CR 107.1.c] so it goes to its controller's base.

Since the equipment is still controlled by its original owner, they can also use a unit with Weaponmaster to pull it back, even while it remains attached - attached cards can still be chosen by game effects. [CR 718.5.b] [CR 821.1.c]

entries.question: What happens to attached equipment when a unit dies?
entries.text:
The equipment detaches and remains at the unit's last location, recalling if at a battlefield.

When a unit with attached equipment dies, the equipment detaches and remains at the location the unit occupied before dying. [CR 719.5] [CR 435.4.b]

If that location is a battlefield, the detached equipment will be recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [CR 435.4.a]
If that location is the controller's base, the equipment simply remains there.

entries.question: What happens if a repeated spell is countered?
entries.text:
The entire spell is countered, including all repeated instructions.

Repeat does not create a second instance of the spell on the chain.
Instead, it modifies how the spell resolves by executing its instructions an additional time. [CR 820.1.d.1]

When a spell is countered, it does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [CR 425.1.a]
Since the spell never resolves, none of its instructions are executed, whether they came from Repeat or not.

entries.question: When do I decide whether to pay for Repeat?
entries.text:
You must decide whether to pay a spell's Repeat cost when you play the spell, not later.

When you play a spell with Repeat, you follow the normal process for playing a card: [CR 353]
1. First, you put the spell onto the chain [CR 354]
2. Then, you make relevant choices, [CR 355] including whether or not you will Repeat it [CR 355.1] [CR 820.1.d]
3. Next, you determine its total cost. [CR 356]
If you chose to Repeat the spell, you apply the Repeat cost as an Optional Additional Cost [CR 356.2] [CR 356.2.b] [CR 356.2.b.1] [CR 820.1.d]
4. Finally, you complete the remaining steps of playing the card to finalize the spell

This means you cannot put a spell on the chain, pass priority to see what happens, and then decide whether to Repeat it later.
The decision must be made upfront during finalization.

callouts.title: Example
callouts.text:
You put Blood Rush, a spell with Repeat 1 energy, that says "Give a unit Assault 2 this turn.", onto the chain.
 Before anyone can respond, you must decide: are you paying the 1 energy to Repeat it and give Assault 2 twice to units, or not?
 Once you've made this choice and paid costs, the spell is finalized.
 Your opponent can now respond with priority, but your Repeat decision is locked in.
